## Abstract

An adaptive volume-of-fluid (VOF) framework, specifically developed for efficient and accurate solutions of multi-scale compressible two-phase flow problems, is devised. The method extends a recently developed space-time adaptive framework for compressible single phase flows, characterized by its combination of a tree-based grid refinement and a local time integration scheme for compressible two-phase flows. Emphasis is put on devising accurate and robust numerical schemes based on dynamically evolving asynchronous grid cells that arises from the space-time adaptivity. These asynchronous schemes also offer solutions to critical challenges in two-phase flows such as dealing with the non-conservative terms, large density ratios and surface tension forces. Moreover, in order to counteract numerical diffusion, an improved interface compression scheme is devised, which demonstrates the capability of preserving the sharpness of fluid interfaces at reduced computational cost. Collectively, these schemes establish a comprehensive novel approach for simulating complex two-phase flows. The efficacy of the solver is substantiated through a series of challenging 1D, 2D and 3D test cases, including capillary oscillation and shock bubble/droplet interactions.
Dealing with them numerically under the context of adaptive space-time discretization becomes even more challenging.

This paper presents a dynamic space-time adaptive algebraic VOF solver for compressible two-phase flows that offers several novel contributions. First, it extends a previously developed space-time adaptive framework for single-phase flows [30], which combines quad-/octree AMR with the adaptive conservative time integration (ACTI) scheme [31], [32], [33], [34], to the more challenging multiphase system. This extension requires incorporation of surface tension effects into the flux discretization schemes and the development of accurate, robust treatments for non-conservative source terms on a non-uniform, asynchronous grid. Second, an artificial compression method is introduced to sharpen the fluid interface. Compared with existing approaches, the proposed scheme is simpler, easier to implement, and maintains high effectiveness and robustness, as demonstrated in several challenging cases.

The paper is structured as follows: The mathematical model is discussed in Section 2 followed by the space-time adaptive numerical scheme in Section 3. The novel interface compression scheme is introduced in Section 4 and four test cases are investigated in Section 5. Finally, the paper closes with concluding remarks and a brief outlook in Section 6.

## Abstract

The main aim of the current work is to apply the Roe+Lax–Friedrichs (LF) hybrid entropy-stable scheme to the simulation of the three-dimensional ambient solar wind. The governing equations for the solar wind flow and magnetic field utilize the entropy-consistent nine-wave magnetic field divergence diminishing ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations, which are symmetric and Galilean invariant with some nonconservative terms proportional to the divergence of magnetic field or the gradient of the Lagrange multiplier ψ. By using solenoidality-preserving and non-negativity-preserving reconstruction, the divergence error is further constrained, and the densities and pressures are reliably guaranteed. Moreover, the entropy is used as an auxiliary equation to completely avoid the appearance of negative pressure, which is independent of any numerical flux and can be retrofit into any MHD equations straightforwardly. All the properties referred to above make the newly developed scheme more handy and robust to cope with the high Mach number or low plasma β situations. After the experiments of the entropy consistency and the robustness of the proposed entropy-stable scheme through two simple tests, we carry out the simulation of the large-scale solar wind structures for Carrington Rotation 2183 (CR 2183) in a six-component grid system with the initial potential field obtained from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager magnetogram by retaining spherical harmonics of degree 50. The comparisons of the numerical results with the remote sensing observations and in situ data show that the new model has the capability to produce structured solar wind.
